subject: pair-implementer
reason: Buttons per status, the successful cancel and the in-flight disabled button all work in the browser, but when the ordering API is unreachable the cancel post returns a bare 500 error page because the list load in OnInitializedAsync is not guarded. The 409 path could only be checked in code because this stack's API does not return 409.

items.reason: With the ordering API stopped, clicking Cancel order makes POST /user/orders return 500 and the page shows only 'Error: 500 Internal Server Error'. On the form post, OnInitializedAsync calls OrderingService.GetOrders() with no try/catch, and its HttpRequestException escapes before CancelOrderAsync can catch it. A timeout fails the same way.
items.fix: Catch HttpRequestException and TaskCanceledException around the GetOrders call in OnInitializedAsync and show the message, or skip the initial load on the cancel post since CancelOrderAsync reloads the list anyway.

items.reason: The cancel PUT goes through the standard resilience retry. When the API answered 500 for an order that was already Paid, the PUT was retried with the same x-requestid and the duplicate request came back 200, so the page showed no message and the order stayed Paid. A 409 is not retried, so this goes away once the API answers 409, but any other 500 on cancel is still hidden.
items.fix: Consider turning off retries for this non-idempotent PUT, or file it as a follow-up for the API's request-id handling.

items.title: Submitted, AwaitingValidation and StockConfirmed orders each show a "Cancel order" button
covers: AC1: Submitted, AwaitingValidation or StockConfirmed order rows have a "Cancel order" button
items.reason: AC1 names three statuses that must offer the button; if one were missing from the cancellable set, the shopper could not cancel an unpaid order. One case for all three because it is one rule observed on one page. E2E because the button only exists in the rendered WebApp page and the statuses come from the real Ordering API.

items.title: Paid, Shipped and Cancelled orders show no "Cancel order" button
covers: AC1: Orders that are Paid, Shipped or Cancelled have no "Cancel order" button
items.reason: AC1's negative half: offering cancel on a paid, shipped or already cancelled order would invite an action the story forbids ("as long as it has not been paid"). Separate from TC-CANC-1-01 because it guards the opposite side of the status rule. E2E because only the rendered page shows whether the button exists.

items.title: Cancelling a Submitted order shows it as Cancelled without an error
covers: AC2: clicking Cancel order on a Submitted order shows it as Cancelled without an error
Code map AC2: list reloaded after the cancel
items.reason: AC2 is the story's main flow: UI form → WebApp OrderingService → `PUT /api/orders/cancel` → domain → reloaded list. A break anywhere would leave the order Submitted or show an error page. E2E is the only layer that runs the whole chain; the extra API read proves the status was persisted, not just rendered.

items.title: A just-placed order cancelled before processing stays Cancelled after the processors have run
covers: AC2: the order stays Cancelled; it never becomes Paid afterwards
items.reason: AC2 requires that a cancelled order is never charged. The real risk is the background pipeline (OrderProcessor grace period → stock validation → PaymentProcessor) picking up a cancelled order and marking it Paid. Only the test stack runs those processors, so this must be e2e with a real order placed through checkout; a seeded order would not exercise the event chain.

items.title: Setting a cancelled order to Paid leaves it Cancelled
covers: AC2: it never becomes Paid afterwards
Deviation: Order.SetPaidStatus() only moves an order from StockConfirmed
items.reason: AC2's "never becomes Paid" rests on one domain rule (the notes say no new code was added for it). A late payment-succeeded event for a cancelled order calls `Order.SetPaidStatus()`; if that rule regressed, the shopper would be charged. A unit test pins the rule cheaply and deterministically, complementing the slower e2e case TC-CANC-1-04.

items.title: Cancelling a StockConfirmed order shows it as Cancelled
covers: Story: cancel as long as it has not been paid
items.reason: StockConfirmed is the last status before Paid, so it is the boundary of "as long as it has not been paid". AC1 offers the button there; if the domain refused the cancel, the shopper would see a button that fails. E2E because the outcome is the rendered row after the full UI → API → domain round trip.

items.title: Cancelling an AwaitingValidation order shows it as Cancelled
covers: Story: cancel as long as it has not been paid
items.reason: AC1 shows the button on AwaitingValidation orders, the status an order sits in while stock is checked. A button that is shown but fails would break the story's promise. Separate from TC-CANC-1-03 and -06 because each status takes its own path through `Order.SetCancelledStatus()`. E2E for the same reason as those cases.

items.title: Cancelling an order that was paid after the page loaded shows "This order can no longer be cancelled." and keeps it Paid
covers: AC3: order paid since My orders was opened → "This order can no longer be cancelled.", keeps Paid, no error page
items.reason: AC3 covers the race between the shopper's stale page and the payment pipeline. The risks: the order is cancelled after payment (shopper charged for a cancelled order) or the shopper gets an error page. E2E because the stale page, the WebApp's handling of the API refusal and the rendered message all have to work together. The status change is made directly in the database so the test controls exactly when the order becomes Paid and no status-change event refreshes the page first.

items.title: bob's cancel request for alice's order is refused and the order stays Submitted
covers: AC4: bob's request to cancel alice's order is refused (403 or 404) and her order keeps its status
items.reason: AC4 limits cancelling to the order's owner. Before this story `PUT /api/orders/cancel` cancelled any order number, so any signed-in user could cancel another shopper's order. The case needs a saved order, which the Ordering functional host cannot hold, so it runs as API calls on the test stack (e2e layer), as the project context prescribes.

items.title: bob cannot cancel alice's order by putting alice's identity in the request body
covers: AC4: a shopper can cancel only their own orders
Code map AC4: BuyerIdentityGuid cannot be set from the body
items.reason: AC4's ownership check compares the order's buyer with an identity carried on the command. If that identity could be supplied in the JSON body, bob could name alice and bypass the rule entirely. This guards the trust boundary separately from TC-CANC-1-09, which sends a plain body. API calls on the test stack (e2e) because the order must be saved.

items.title: My orders still shows each order's number, date, total and status
covers: AC5: number, date, total and status are shown on My orders as today
items.reason: AC5 is a regression guard: the story adds a column of actions to every row, which could shift or drop the existing columns. Seeded orders with known values make each cell checkable. E2E because the columns exist only in the rendered page.

items.title: Placing an order through checkout still works and the new order is listed as Submitted
covers: AC5: placing an order works as today
AC1: a new Submitted order shows the Cancel order button
items.reason: AC5 requires checkout to be unaffected; the story changed the Ordering API's command handling and the My orders page that checkout lands on. The full checkout flow only runs end to end through the WebApp on the test stack.
